title: Gifts to City departments from parties the same department pays or licenses
question: Who gives money, goods and services to City departments, and which donors hold a contract, grant, permit or lease with the department they gave to?
finding: Departments reported 1,933 gifts valued at $39.7 million between 2024-11-01 and 2026-10-31; Police (POL) received $15.3 million and Mayor's Office (MYR) $7.7 million. 93 donor organizations, giving $6.4 million (16% of the value), hold a contract, grant, permit or lease with the receiving department by the department's own entry on the form or by its payment record; the largest is San Francisco Symphony ($2.2 million to Arts Commission (ART)). For 14 of them a contract with that department began within a year of a gift.
how: Every line of the departments' monthly gift reports (the form asks the department to describe any contract, licence, permit or other financial interest the donor has with it). A donor is listed when the department wrote such a tie on the form, or when the payment file shows the same department paying a payee of the same name $5,000 or more in fiscal 2025 to 2027. Contract numbers written on the form, and contracts in the contract table under the donor's name with that department, supply the contract and its start date; 'within a year' means a contract start within 365 days either side of a gift. A remark in the form's 'other financial interest' box that names no contract, grant, permit, licence or lease is not treated as a tie. 7 lines are the form's blank template (donor 'Name is required.', $50,000 each) and are left out. Individuals and donors not recognisable as organizations are counted (1,048 donors, 50 of them with a tie) and not listed.
limits: Giving to a department must be reported exactly like this, and is often simple generosity; most of the listed ties are the ordinary relationship between a department and the organizations built around it (resident arts companies giving tickets to the War Memorial, a hospital foundation, a grantee donating to an event). A gift near a contract date is a coincidence in time, not evidence that one caused the other, and many contracts listed were competitively bid. Donor and payee are matched by name, and a donor typed two ways on the forms appears twice. The source looks incomplete rather than the conduct: when a department amends a month, the list keeps only the latest filing's lines, so 53 earlier filings whose cover pages total $3.6 million have no lines here and some of their gifts may be missing. The reports begin in November 2024; earlier gifts are not in this file. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days.
